slice_results.behavior_summary: At import-time, the code instantiates Leaderboard objects with different style types, generates PNG images via canvas buffers, and writes these images to local files under the ./test directory using fs.writeFileSync, resulting in the creation of styled leaderboard image files on disk.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code uses standard Node.js APIs (fs.writeFileSync, path.resolve) to generate and save PNG images to local disk. This behavior is typical for applications that generate image files dynamically and does not involve obfuscation, arbitrary code execution, external downloads, or attempts to access sensitive files. Compared to the known malicious patterns, there is no evidence of obfuscated filesystem access (Example 1), no arbitrary code execution or sensitive file reading (Example 2), and no hidden external binary execution or resource hijacking (Example 3). The code’s intent appears to be legitimate image generation and file writing within a controlled directory, which is a common and benign use case.

malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Obfuscation may be used in proprietary code to protect intellectual property, but not in open-source utility libraries where transparency is expected.

Obfuscation of standard library access
Helper functions that mask real API calls

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, when user-supplied Markdown is processed for PDF export, the code executes arbitrary JavaScript via the gray-matter front matter parser, reads the contents of /flag.txt using Node.js fs.readFileSync, and injects the file contents into the CSS of the generated PDF, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive data to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code abuses the Markdown front matter feature to execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server, which is highly abnormal and dangerous. It directly accesses sensitive files using Node.js APIs and exposes their contents to the user through the generated PDF.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, Markdown-to-PDF conversion should only process markup and never execute arbitrary code. The expected behavior is safe, deterministic rendering of user input, not server-side code execution or file access.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Server-side code execution via Markdown front matter is never legitimate in production environments. In rare, highly controlled admin-only scenarios, such features might be used for advanced templating, but never with untrusted or user-supplied input.

Arbitrary JavaScript execution during Markdown parsing

Lack of input sanitization or code execution restrictions in Markdown processing

package_info.why_malicious: The md-to-pdf package (version 4.1.0) is critically vulnerable because it uses the gray-matter library with JavaScript engine support enabled by default. This allows attackers to inject arbitrary JavaScript code via Markdown front matter, resulting in remote code execution (RCE) on the server. Exploitation enables attackers to read sensitive files (such as /flag.txt) and exfiltrate their contents, violating core security boundaries.

attack_chain.leads_to: Server parses the Markdown and executes the embedded JavaScript code.

attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive data (flag) is loaded into memory during document generation.

attack_chain.leads_to: Flag is exfiltrated to the attacker via the exported PDF file.

The package copies the README and structure of the real 'chalk' package to deceive users and compromise their data.

attack_chain.action: User installs or imports the malicious 'chalk-node' package, triggering execution of index.esm.js.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sentry is initialized with a hardcoded DSN and obfuscated file system access helpers are set up, preparing the environment for data exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: Whenever console.log is called, the overridden function reads files from a '../data' directory and checks log arguments for sensitive patterns.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive file contents and log data are prepared for exfiltration to the attacker's Sentry instance.

attack_chain.action: File contents and/or log data are sent to the attacker's Sentry instance, using chunked messages and obfuscated prefixes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives exfiltrated data; user remains unaware due to silent error handling and obfuscated code.

behavioral_signatures: Obfuscated access to Node.js fs module methods (readdirSync, existsSync, readFileSync) via dynamically constructed function names
Overriding of console.log with hidden file system access and network exfiltration side effects
File system reads from '../data' directory triggered by logging activity
Network requests to Sentry or other telemetry endpoints with hardcoded DSNs at import-time
Silent error handling (empty catch blocks) in code paths handling sensitive data or network operations
Freezing of the console object to prevent further modification
file_indicators: Presence of index.esm.js with obfuscated and minified code
Unexpected initialization of @sentry/node in utility packages
References to '../data' directory access in code
Obfuscated helper functions for fs module access
network_indicators: Outbound requests to o4505703178960896.ingest.sentry.io or similar Sentry DSNs
Unusual volume of Sentry.captureMessage calls from utility packages
Data exfiltration patterns using chunked messages and obfuscated prefixes in Sentry events
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages that override console.log or other standard output functions, especially if they access the filesystem or send data to external telemetry services. Flag any use of obfuscated or dynamically constructed method names for core modules (e.g., fs['readFileSync']). Alert on unexpected initialization of @sentry/node or similar telemetry SDKs in utility libraries. Watch for outbound network requests to hardcoded Sentry DSNs or other suspicious endpoints, particularly if accompanied by chunked or obfuscated payloads. Use static analysis to detect empty catch blocks in code that handles sensitive data or network operations. Scan for references to '../data' directory access and freezing of the console object in package code.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, shortly after import, the code initiates a delayed execution using setTimeout, performs an external geolocation API request, parses the response to determine the user's country, and if the country is Russia or Belarus, recursively calls a file deletion function on multiple directory levels, resulting in destructive file overwrites.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code makes an unsolicited external geolocation API request and, based on the result, triggers recursive file overwrite operations targeting the entire filesystem. This is a clear indicator of a targeted, destructive payload.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate IPC package should not perform geolocation checks or attempt to overwrite user files under any circumstances. The expected behavior is to provide inter-process communication utilities, not to execute destructive actions based on user location.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Geolocation checks may be used for regional feature toggling or compliance, but never to trigger destructive file operations. Recursive file deletion is only appropriate in uninstallers or cleanup tools, and only with explicit user consent.
key_indicators: Automated geolocation API request at runtime
Conditional logic targeting specific countries (Russia, Belarus)
Recursive invocation of file overwrite function across multiple directory levels
Destructive file operations triggered without user interaction

package_info.why_malicious: The package was intentionally altered by its maintainer to include code that, upon execution, checks the user's geolocation via an external API. If the user is located in Russia or Belarus, the code recursively overwrites files across the filesystem with a heart emoji, resulting in widespread and deliberate data destruction. This constitutes a targeted sabotage attack, which is entirely outside the scope of legitimate package behavior.

attack_chain.action: On package installation or import, the malicious code in dao/ssl-geospec.js is loaded and scheduled for execution via setTimeout.
attack_chain.leads_to: Geolocation check and potential execution of destructive payload

attack_chain.action: The code performs an external geolocation API request to determine if the user is located in Russia or Belarus.
attack_chain.leads_to: Conditional execution of recursive file overwrite function

attack_chain.action: If the user is in a targeted country, the code recursively attempts to overwrite all files on the system with a heart emoji.
attack_chain.leads_to: Destruction of user and system data

attack_chain.action: In related packages (peacenotwar, oneday-test), the code writes a protest message file to user Desktop and OneDrive directories.
attack_chain.leads_to: Display of unsolicited political/protest message in user-accessible locations

behavioral_signatures: JavaScript packages that make runtime geolocation API requests and subsequently perform recursive filesystem operations or file overwrites
Recursive file overwrite attempts targeting user and system directories, especially with static content (e.g., heart emoji)
Creation of unsolicited files with political or protest content in user Desktop or OneDrive directories
file_indicators: dao/ssl-geospec.js
WITH-LOVE-FROM-AMERICA.txt
Unusual file writes to ~/Desktop, ~/OneDrive, ~/OneDrive/Desktop
network_indicators: https://api.ipgeolocation.io/ipgeo?apiKey=ae511e1627824a968aaaa758a5309154
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for JavaScript packages that initiate external geolocation API requests at runtime, especially if followed by recursive filesystem operations or file overwrites. Flag any package that writes unsolicited files to user Desktop or OneDrive directories, or that contains the file dao/ssl-geospec.js. Alert on the presence of WITH-LOVE-FROM-AMERICA.txt in user directories. Correlate destructive file operations or unusual file creation with recent package updates or new dependencies to identify malicious activity.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code initiates an HTTPS GET request to a remote server to download a file named 'initial.png', decodes the base64 content, and executes it using eval, resulting in immediate remote code execution and enabling the delivery of a stage 2 payload.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs a network request to a hardcoded external domain at import-time, decodes the response as base64, and executes it dynamically with eval. This pattern is a textbook example of remote code execution and malware staging, as it allows the attacker to deliver and run arbitrary code on the victim's system without user interaction.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate CORS parser should not perform any network requests or execute remote code during import. Such behavior is entirely outside the scope of expected functionality for a CORS utility.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic code loading may be used in plugin systems or self-updating frameworks, but never in a CORS utility, and never at import-time without user consent.
key_indicators: Import-time network request to external domain
Decoding and eval of remote content
No user interaction required for execution
Hardcoded URL to suspicious domain

package_info.why_malicious: The package is explicitly designed to act as a dropper for platform-specific backdoors. It abuses import-time execution to fetch and run remote code disguised as PNG images, which are actually malicious payloads. The code uses steganography and dynamic code execution to implant persistent malware on both Windows and Unix systems, violating user trust and security boundaries by enabling remote code execution, persistence, and system compromise.

attack_chain.action: Initial package installation or import triggers a network request to download and execute remote code from 'initial.png' using eval.
attack_chain.leads_to: Stage 2 payload execution

attack_chain.action: Stage 2 code, decoded from 'initial.png', determines the operating system and downloads platform-specific disguised binaries (DLLs for Windows, ELF/Mach-O for Unix) from the remote server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware drop and execution

attack_chain.action: The malware is written to disk, executed, and persistence is established via registry autorun (Windows) or shell configuration file modification (Unix), resulting in a persistent backdoor and system compromise.
attack_chain.leads_to: Backdoor persistence and full system compromise

behavioral_signatures: Import-time or install-time network requests to download files with image extensions (e.g., .png) from hardcoded external domains
Decoding and dynamic execution (eval) of remote content at import-time
Writing and executing binaries from files with image extensions (.png) in system or temporary directories
Establishing persistence via registry autorun keys (Windows) or shell configuration file modifications (Unix)
file_indicators: index.js containing minified or obfuscated one-liner network/eval logic
Downloaded files named *.png but containing non-image binary content
/var/tmp/logd (Unix malware dropper path)
C:/ProgramData/thumbs.db (Windows malware dropper path)
Modifications to .zshrc (Unix) or registry autorun keys (Windows)
network_indicators: api.jz-aws.info (all subdomains and paths)
Unusual PNG file downloads from non-image hosting domains, especially during package import or install
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that initiate network requests at import or install time, particularly those downloading files with image extensions but containing non-image content. Flag code that decodes and executes remote content via eval. Watch for creation of binaries in temporary or system locations (e.g., /var/tmp/logd, C:/ProgramData/thumbs.db) and persistence mechanisms such as registry autorun entries or shell configuration file modifications. Network monitoring should alert on connections to api.jz-aws.info and similar suspicious domains, especially when associated with package installation or import events.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code loads legitimate speed test modules to provide expected functionality, while simultaneously downloading and executing a mining binary in the background, which connects to a mining pool and hijacks system resources for mining.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code blends legitimate speed test functionality with hidden malicious mining activity, a classic trojanization technique. The malicious process is launched in the background to avoid user detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A speed test utility should not execute unrelated binaries or initiate background mining processes while providing legitimate functionality.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate use for this behavior exists in a speed test utility. Blending benign and malicious code is a hallmark of trojanized packages.
key_indicators: Blending of legitimate and malicious code in the same file
Background mining process launched alongside expected functionality
External binary download and execution
Outbound connection to mining pool

package_info.package_versions: all versions published by user 'trendava' before Jan 18, 2023
package_info.why_malicious: These packages impersonate legitimate internet speed testing utilities but instead deploy cryptocurrency miners, covertly hijacking system resources for unauthorized mining operations. The packages employ multiple evasion techniques, including downloading mining binaries from external sources, embedding miners, dynamically retrieving mining pool addresses, and blending malicious activity with legitimate functionality to avoid detection.

attack_chain.action: User installs or imports the malicious NPM package, believing it to be a legitimate speed test utility.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code execution at import-time

attack_chain.action: Malicious code in index.js executes at import-time, downloading a mining binary from an external source (such as GitLab or an external IP).
attack_chain.leads_to: Binary is made executable and launched

attack_chain.action: The mining binary is executed, connecting to a cryptocurrency mining pool (address may be hardcoded or dynamically retrieved from an external source).
attack_chain.leads_to: System resources are hijacked for mining

attack_chain.action: In some variants, legitimate speed test functionality is provided to avoid suspicion and maintain user trust.
attack_chain.leads_to: User is unaware of background mining activity

behavioral_signatures: NPM package executes code at import-time or install-time, triggering process execution without user interaction
Downloads and executes external binaries from untrusted sources such as GitLab or direct IP addresses
Initiates outbound connections to known mining pool addresses or suspicious IPs, including WebSocket connections
Blends legitimate speed test functionality with hidden mining activity in the same codebase
file_indicators: index.js containing exec, wget, curl, chmod, or nohup commands
Presence of downloaded binaries named 'data', 'los', or 'miner' in the package directory
Unexpected use of process execution functions (e.g., exec) in JavaScript files of speed test utilities
network_indicators: Connections to gitlab.com/parsnekamser/clouds/-/raw/main/* for binary downloads
Outbound connections to mining pool addresses such as eu.kaspa.k1pool.com:15555 and 51.222.96.66:80
Dynamic retrieval of mining pool addresses from external IPs via HTTP or curl
WebSocket connections to suspicious IPs for mining activity
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor NPM package installations and imports for scripts that download and execute external binaries, especially from non-standard or untrusted sources. Flag packages that initiate outbound connections to known mining pools or suspicious IPs, or use exec/spawn to run shell commands. Inspect for blended code that provides expected speed test functionality while launching background processes. Use static and dynamic analysis to detect unexpected process creation, file downloads, and network activity during package installation or import. Correlate presence of binaries named 'data', 'los', or 'miner' with suspicious process and network behavior.
